utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today is Thursday, 6 November 2008. Good morning, Witness. Good morning to all the OTP representatives, good morning, Mr. Seselj, and good morning to all the people helping us out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I still have a few questions to ask you, and I am now getting to the following question. You told us you testified in the so-called Vukovar trial, in the Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic trial. I assume that you were

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: told us that you had reported to Colonel Mrksic what you had seen in Ovcara, and I assume that this may have been challenged by Colonel Mrksic. As far as you can remember, do you remember whether the lawyer for Colonel Mrksic cross-examined you on this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was his case? What did Colonel Mrksic say about the fact that you had apparently reported to the colonel about what you had seen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not say anything about that. They just noted what I said and did not dispute it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we infer from that that Colonel Mrksic did not agree with you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty whether he agreed with me or not, but I know that the Defence did not ask me any questions about my reporting to Mrksic. We talked about other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you took up command in December in Vukovar, and that is a few days only after the fall of Vukovar. We know because we heard several witnesses in this respect, but we had a witness just before you yesterday. The witness said that she was taken prisoner and taken to the - I can't remember the name - I think it's Sremska Mitrovica prison. So she was taken to that prison, where she was examined, interrogated, by a so-called Colonel Branko as part of an investigation that was underway. So there's no doubt about it. The JNA did investigate by interviewing people. As far as you know, was there a so-called Command investigation - that is the military term for it - as to the events in Vukovar; and as part of your duties and responsibility as the Vukovar commander in December, did you have the visit of investigators who wanted to know and ask you what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody came to talk to me specifically about these matters, but I did hear, at the meeting with Mrksic, that he said investigative authorities would come from Belgrade, and somebody from the prosecution would come, that they would investigate and gather facts about it. He even said that accommodation would be provided -- should be provided for these people. This must have begun while Colonel Mrksic was still there. How this whole thing developed from that on, I don't know, but I know it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're telling me that before he left, Colonel Mrksic told you that investigators were about to come and that you had to do all that was necessary to accommodate them, to put them up. So, obviously, you do confirm that there was an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Colonel. I'm not exactly sure of your testimony. Could you be clear about whether, to your knowledge, an investigation was ever carried out? Did these people come from Belgrade, as Colonel Mrksic had said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that just to me. He said it at the meeting of commanders and commanding officers of the brigade, that accommodation be provided to these people. I saw some of these people, but I didn't know them, because I had come to the area from Slovenia. I didn't know any of these people, but I know that some action was taken. In what scope, for how long, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And did you ever hear of the results of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answering my fellow Judge's question, you said that you saw the investigators come, but that you didn't know them. But you saw them with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them. I saw two or three persons, and I was told that they had come from a court in Belgrade, but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Were they in military uniforms? Did they show signs of ranks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw one of them in uniform. I believe he had the rank of lieutenant-colonel or colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the JNA military rules, whenever there is an investigation on command exercise, does the investigation have to be carried out by somebody whose rank is higher than the one who's being investigated or not.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, among those people who came, there were some of equal rank to those in the superior command, so it was a rule, but it didn't always happen in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, something else. You were in Vukovar in December. Where was your office, precisely, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vukovar, my Command was first in Negoslavci village; and later, when the Guard Brigade moved to Belgrade, the Command was moved to the barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had an office in the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In December, I suppose there was still Croatian residents in Vukovar who would go back to their homes, or was it so that there was no Croatian resident left?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Croats who were going back to their homes, and to the extent of our ability, we helped them and protected them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So there were Croats who returned to their homes, and you did your job, the job you had to do as a commander. We know that there are 200 people -- that 200 people left the hospital and went to Ovcara, and we now know that most of them were killed there. Based on family ties, theoretically, it could be that these 200 individuals had relatives, relatives who went back to their homes and found that their relatives, be they brothers or cousins, are no longer there. Did families go to the Vukovar barracks to say, "Look, my relative," who was a soldier or a civilian, "disappeared. We don't know anything about him or her. Can you tell us, give us any information about what happened to him?" Did people go to see you -- well, you or officers, or whoever was at the gate checking people when they came in, did anybody go to seek information? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anyone coming to see me, but I don't know about my COs and commanding officers. I don't know whether anybody came to see them to inquire about their missing relatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had no information at all. You stayed in Vukovar until when, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 28th February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 28th of February, 1992. Just one detail. Before you took up command in December, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were a lieutenant-colonel. When you took up command in Vukovar, did you keep that rank or did you become a colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I kept my rank. But that year was the time for my regular promotion, because colonels and generals are promoted on the 22nd December. My whole unit was supposed to go back to Kragujevac on the 13th or the 14th, so it was left for that day so that my promotion coincide with the return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you promoted, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13th January 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 13th of January, 1992. When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left active service on the 1st January 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you not become a general?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't depend on me. I would have liked to become a general, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, how long did a JNA colonel have to wait before he became a general?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stricter rules were in place at the time than today. Somebody could spend five, six, and ten years as a colonel without ever being promoted to general. I spent ten years as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these were the questions I had for you, based on the statement you gave and details we had to seek. I'm sure my fellow Judges have questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Colonel, I have just one question to put to you regarding the relations between the JNA and the paramilitaries or the volunteers. I should perhaps reassure you that, of course, you are not on trial here, so I'm asking a few questions in relation to this aspect and I hope that you will give me a frank answer. The question I have relates to the situation that you described to us yesterday, when you said that towards the end of the day of I think it was the 20th of November, you passed by Ovcara, and you saw buses coming and prisoners being taken out of the buses and having to walk through a gauntlet and being driven into the hangar. I think you also told us that you stopped and went out to see what was happening, because this was news to you. You had not heard that anything was going to happen here, so you wanted to know what was going on. The question I have is, first of all: Were you, as you stepped out of the car, the highest-ranking officer on the spot? My second question - think about it - is: If you were, could you have done anything to stop it? Could you have called these soldiers to order and stopped the mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought at first that I was the officer with the highest rank there, but a couple of minutes later, I realised I wasn't. There was a colonel there. I'd never said his name, but I said what he was doing. It's obvious that he was watching the situation from outside. I approached him, and I asked him, "What is going on here? Please help me restore some order here so that these people are not mistreated." When I said that, he just got into his car and left. There was a commanding officer from the superior command in the hangar with a high rank, and I realised I didn't know what was going on, but commanding officers were there, and so that should have been all right, in my eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If you want to go into private session for you to tell us who these gentlemen were, we can do so, but I'm a bit interested in knowing more about the situation at the Ovcara farm during the time you were there. You just told me that when you arrived, you addressed yourself to a colonel, who didn't answer your question and who left immediately after. So, from that point on, you could perhaps have been the highest-ranking officer, except that you told me that there was another officer who still was also a colonel, thus having a higher rank than yours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that one did not have an equal rank, he had a lower rank, but I don't know about the others. There were more people there whom I didn't know with improper clothing, without caps, so I didn't know who they were. I did not know these people. I'm telling you, I came from Slovenia. I saw those officers in that group, in that place, for the first time. That colonel I saw, I saw him when he was leaving the hangar. He was standing on the side, and I approached him as a military man to ask him what was going on. He wasn't far away. He was watching the whole situation. I don't know to this day what his name was. I can venture a guess, but I don't want to guess. There was another officer with a higher rank than me who was following the situation, the chief of staff. I had not seen him there, but he later told me he had been there. So both of them were higher in rank than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have to put a hypothetical question to you, and that is: If you had attempted to stop the madness after the colonel had left, would you have succeeded?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, looking back, first of all, he left, but other commanding officers from that unit stayed. I alone couldn't have done it, because I had no strength and no resources to stop it. I think I had done my maximum, protecting those people at the outset. The Command that was -- my Command that was nearby and those people, I did all I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But how does it work? I mean, I would imagine that it is the highest-ranking officer at the spot who has the command. So, if you thought that you were the highest-ranking officer after the colonel had left, the thought might have occurred to you that you should simply put a stop to this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still wasn't the highest-ranking officer. There was a chief of staff there, a deputy commander of the operative group, who was senior to me, not in rank but in position, and his unit was carrying that out. His men were involved. You can't do anything in another unit when senior officers are present, and you don't know what they're doing, what their assignment is. I had done my best, once I saw those people there. I maintained then and I maintain now that nobody believed at that moment that something could happen of the kind that actually happened later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So am I to understand that what you were able to observe at that time at Ovcara was that everything that went on was being well controlled and well commanded by a senior JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were senior to me and their command was senior to me; although, I did not see them at the first time in that crowd in that complexity of the situation, the constant movement, but I saw later and found out later that they were there. Now, how they managed it, I don't know. I couldn't evaluate that because that assignment was not known to me. It was being carried out without our knowledge, without the involvement of our men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I realise that you must have been in a terrible dilemma, because I think you have told us already that what you saw was, from a strictly legal point of view, unacceptable. You saw civilians being mistreated, and no soldier of the JNA should engage in such activity under any circumstance, and this is why you put your first question to the colonel, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked for assistance to be given to those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But no assistance was given. The colonel sort of just left and did nothing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So I return to my question. Could you have done anything to stop it when you saw that obviously the colonel did not intend to stop the mistreatment? Did it occur to you that you should then persist, or was it your feeling that even if you tried, you would have been unable to achieve anything? Were you afraid?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't afraid, but I thought there were commanding officers there from the superior command; and in my eyes, that was some sort of guarantee of security and protection for those people. These people from the superior command continued to be there, including that chief of staff who was watching the situation. He even stated, himself, that he watched me grappling with these soldiers, trying to prevent them from beating the prisoners as they were coming into the hangar. But the big unknown to me was who these people were, how come they were there, who brought them. But when I got into the hangar and I saw a group of people, among them a ranking officer, I logically thought he was there, he would make sure there was order, he must have some kind of assignment, although I didn't know which. Then order was restored in the hangar temporarily while I was there. Mistreatment stopped, prisoners were not beaten anymore, there were no insults and ethnic slurs. There was some verbal threats, but not mistreatment. Prisoners were put on one side and separated from members of the Territorial Defence. That is the situation that I left in the hangar when I departed. I don't know what happened later. I don't know how responsible they were for later actions. Maybe they helped cordon off the prisoners and restore order to the hangar. When this order was restored, I left the hangar, went to my command post, and informed my superior officer what I had seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did the mistreatment in the hangar stop because of your presence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can say that it was because of me alone. It is true, I did my best to prevent this sort of thing going on, but there were other commanding officers there. I didn't check, there and then, who was doing what and who was issuing orders to whom to do what, and how the attempts were made to stop the violence. One thing is certain, it did stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One follow-up question. You told us that the deputy commander of the operative group was there. Going back to your written statement, paragraph 31, your public statement, I see the name of Major Vukasinovic. Was he the deputy commander in question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was the deputy chief of security, which means Major Sljivancanin's deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When talking about this deputy commander, you say that in the chain of command, he was above you. Can you give us his name in open session, or would you rather we moved into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what his name was. I did see the man, I know what he looks like, I know that he was a colonel by rank, but I don't know exactly what his role was or function. I do assume that he was one of the assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why is it that you do not know the name of that colonel who was a member of the unit, together with Colonel Mrksic? Why is it that you do not know his name, or is it that you forgot his name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I forgot. I think you haven't quite understood. Those people from Operations Group South, or the Guards Brigade, if you like, are people that I came across for the very first time in my life in that area. We'd never been in touch. I had recently arrived from a different area. I'd never seen those people before. I met my own commanding officer, I met the assistant commander for logistics, I met the chief of security, and I knew about the chief of staff. I didn't know about anyone else because I didn't contact any of the other people. Perhaps I set eyes on them several times, perhaps I could ID them, but I have no idea what their names were. I didn't know then, I didn't know later, I don't know now. It is true that we spent some short time together later on. They had left. The Command was a rather large command, and there were a lot of officers whom I just didn't know, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand. Under the military rules and regulations, is the highest-ranking officer in the field the one in charge, the one who commands, the one who has all the authority, all the power; or is it so that if you have a military operation underway, for example, a transfer of prisoners where orders have been given and people have been put in charge of the operation, can an officer, who has nothing to do with the operation, can he take charge of the whole thing, despite the orders, based on the rules in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is no commanding officer, if it is not clear who should do what, I don't mean just a single commanding officer but rather a group of high-ranking officers who were around, then the highest officer present would have been duty-bound to take steps. In this situation, however, there were commanding officers there from the superior command, the highest-ranking officers. There was nothing at all that I could have done bypassing them in that situation. Then another thing I have to note is we had not involved in the preparation or the execution of this task, in terms of taking prisoners away from the hospital. This was something that we were entirely in the dark about until I just chanced on the scene, as it were. Had I not chanced upon the scene that very minute, I probably would have seen nothing at all. I would have learned the next day, as everyone else, those from Negoslavci and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, I asked you if you had communication resources at your disposal, if you had a Motorola, for example, and you said, "No." In your opinion, did this colonel have communication means allowing him to get in touch with the duty officer at the HQ or with Colonel Mrksic? Yes, please answer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the one in the hangar, or those who were in the hangar, what their communication was with their own Command. I don't know about the colonel who was standing outside the hangar, next to the car. Did he have a radio in the car, any sort of communications equipment? Was he in touch with anyone? Not that I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a military setting, isn't there a basic, a fundamental principle that is the following: Under all circumstances, whatever happens, the Command has to be in communication with operational units in the field? They always have to remain in contact. Isn't that a golden rule, in military terms, when it comes to military operations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a rule, a rule which is maintained whenever possible by using communications equipment, vehicles, messengers are sent out and so on and so forth. I don't know how this worked in this specific situation, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me now give the floor to my fellow Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one question only, Witness. For various reasons, I'm not going to put any questions to you about the substance of your testimony, but I'd like to have a clarification regarding the fact that you came here to testify for the Prosecution. I would be interested to know under what circumstances you changed your position, because you told us that in the past you cooperated with one or several Defence teams in the Vukovar trial. So could you please shed some light on this for us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the start of this investigation, I had provided I forget how many statements to the Security Service of the JNA, and then this whole procedure began. So I spoke several times with the attorneys defending the Vukovar three, with the exception of Attorney Borovic. I talked to them two or three times, and I provided information to them, just as I have now to you. That was the extent of it. The next thing I knew, the Prosecution called me and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Borovic was the Defence counsel of which accused?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He defended the accused Radic, and he was the only attorney of the three that I did not speak to. On the other hand, I spoke to Mr. Vasic, on behalf of Mr. Mrksic, and Mr. Lukic, on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin. I had a particularly extensive conversation with Mr. Vasic. I told him everything that I have been telling you here. Eventually, and I'm not sure what the reason was for that, I was dropped. The Prosecution asked me to talk to them, which I did. They asked me some questions, just like you, and then we no longer worked together. I think they were the ones to put a stop to our cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you were moved by a spirit of cooperation with justice, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm having trouble understanding the interpretation. I'm not sure why. It's something with the headset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a problem? Should I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's fine now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I repeat my question? Well, based on what you've just explained to us, it seems that you came here to testify, and that you intended to testify for the Defence case in the Vukovar case, because you were moved by the desire to cooperate with justice. Is this what you're getting at?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me be frank about it. I was not really willing to work with anyone on this, the Defence or the Prosecution. It was simply that I had no choice, so I ended up talking to both. Likewise, it was not my desire to appear here now. I had some peculiar problems, some health problems, but I just wanted to put an end to the uncertainty, both for myself and the environment in which I live, so I decided to end up by coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to Mr. Ferrara. Any redirect, any questions arising out of the Judges' questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Not a question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. There can be no re-examination unless there was cross-examination, to begin with. I wish to point that out for the record, and, of course, you do as you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. This has been recorded on the transcript. Do you have anything to say about this legal issue, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. It is longstanding practice before this Tribunal that re-examination covers the scope of any questions put by the Trial Chamber, in addition to any questions arising from cross-examination, and we want that position put clearly on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, I was asking if you had any questions, and you said, "No questions."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I want to address something to the Trial Chamber concerning the document we discussed yesterday in the incident involving three members of the Leva Supoderica unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: The Prosecution wants to draw your attention to the fact that this document was obtained from the government of Serbia and Montenegro at the time, in response of the official request for assistance of the OTP number 853, and the document was translated at the time by a language assistant in the absence of a CLSS ability to translate it at the time. We agree that there is an omission of Kameni's alleged rank in the English version, but I don't believe this omission should have an impact on the authenticity of the B/C/S original of the document. So I want to put on the record how we got this document. It is in response of the OTP, RFA number 853.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. I'll be giving you the floor in a few seconds. We now have on the record the fact that this document was given to you by the Serbian authorities following an RFA. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara is misinterpreting the substance of that document. He claims that this is a document in relation to an incident involving three members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment. This is simply not true. This is by no means true. The document shows that it was three members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment who were killed. Now, someone who gets killed cannot be said to be involved in anything at all. The incident is about three persons getting killed. Three members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment were the victims of a killing and not those involved in an incident. Nowhere does this document indicate any sort of involvement at all on their part in any sort of incident at all. This is a malicious misinterpretation, as well as this later version about a purported mistranslation. It is quite clear to me that no mistranslation is at stake here, but something altogether different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Trial Chamber has given an MFI number to this document. It's, of course, possible to ask CLSS for a full translation of this document. That's always a possibility. Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree with Mr. Seselj, so it means that three members of the Leva Supoderica unit were still there on the 22nd of December, 1991. That's exactly what I want to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But it would be very useful --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj, one moment before interrupting me. It would be very useful for the Trial Chamber to have a full translation, for the following reason: If I look at the translation in English, I see that three members of the Vukovar TO were killed. That's to be found in the first sentence, that they were killed in Vukovar. They were killed. But if you look at paragraph 3, we see the following: The killed individuals were members of the Leva Supoderica unit. These words of "were members" could be understood as means that they had been members of the unit, but that it was not the case any longer at the time when they were killed, because if you look at paragraph 1 of this same document, you see that they were members of the Vukovar TO. So we need CLSS to provide a translation of this document, because we want to have an accurate translation of the text in B/C/S. Nuances are of the essence here. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wanted to say exactly the same thing that you have just observed, Mr. President. Now we have Mr. Ferrara offering yet another misinterpretation, trying to let you know that on the 23rd of December, the Leva Supoderica Detachment was still around, yet the document does not reflect this. It is just about what you have observed. Members of the Leva Supoderica were there. That's the essence. That's what I was trying to say. Had I known that you would step in, I would not have objected at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, Our case manager has already requested an official translation today of CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. We will therefore have an official translation of this document, and everybody will be able to review that translation; Mr. Seselj, the Prosecutor and the Bench. Colonel, thank you for having testified, as a Prosecution witness, about the events you may have witnessed. I wish you a safe trip home, and I'm going to ask the usher to bring you to the door of this courtroom for you to be able to leave as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's almost 25 past 9.00. I think it's probably best, Mr. Mundis, if you agree to have the break now. We're going to have a 20-minute break, and we'll resume with the last witness for this week. Would you agree with that, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. We are going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have another witness. There are no protective measures been asked for the witness. Is that correct:

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness appears, I do have an observation to make. I must respond to Mr. Mundis' words before the break of the. Mr. Mundis tells the Chamber that it has been a longstanding, established practice before this Tribunal for issues to be considered that were potentially raised by the Trial Chamber during re-examination. Indeed, that is true, such a thing exists in the practice of this Tribunal, but only as far as any questions asked by the Trial Chamber are to do with issues raised during the examination-in-chief or cross-examination. However, it has not so far been recorded for a Defence to waive its right to cross-examination while the Prosecution were granted the right to re-examine. That has never so far been the case; therefore, this interpretation of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is not correct. Just another thing. Just imagine the following situation: For example, we have examination-in-chief, but no cross-examination; or there is cross-examination and then the Judges ask an enormous amount of questions, raising entirely new issues not previously raised. What about the rights of a Defence? Is a Defence then granted the right to additionally cross-examine? This raises a whole lot of new problems, and that is why I believe Mr. Mundis' interpretation to be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have said is now on the record. Yes, I had turned to the Prosecution to ask her whether any specific measures had been asked for the witness. You said there wasn't?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: (redacted) to inquire of the witness regarding the need for protective measures before the beginning of the witness's testimony, since yesterday, on 5th November, during the proofing session, the witness informed the Prosecution that she wished to have protective measures in the form of a pseudonym and image distortion during public testimony, because even though -- Sorry, Your Honours. If we can redact the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be done. Let us move into private session, first of all, to have the witness brought in and then further redaction.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Julka Maretic. I was born in 1942, in Strezimirovci village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were born in 1942. When exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2nd of August, 1942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 2nd of August, 1942. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now retired. But when I was younger, when I got married, I worked at the police station in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had an opportunity to testify before a court of law as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is this going to be the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went twice to Bjelovar to testify just after the war, and this is the first time here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it a trial in Bjelovar; and if so, who was the case about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified to the events in Vocin, what happened when I arrived in Vocin, where I lived, where I worked, what I did, all up until the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you testified, I suppose that there were accused in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was testifying, there were people accused, those who had occupied us in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were the accused convicted or acquitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't tell. Do you remember the names of the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first we accused the Serbs who had occupied us. Later, when the army came from Serbia, they held themselves out to be as Seselj's men, others said they were Arkan's men. We ran away from them, we avoided them, and they were accused of causing us a lot of trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was whether the accused in that trial in which you testified, whether you knew their names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first days when they occupied us, those were our men, locals. They came to our street and convened all the men together. Those were Drago Dobrovic [phoen], and what's his name? I can't remember the other man's name. Drago Dobrovic, I know, and there was another one with him. I know the name, it's just that it eludes me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Drago Dobrovic, he was charged and accused, and you testified in his case. Am I to understand things in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I didn't testify against anybody. I just told the truth and what we experienced in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are not going to dwell on the matter. Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Please be seated. Let me explain how this testimony is going to take place. You've already met with a representative of the OTP before coming into this courtroom. I guess they explained what I'm about to tell you, but I still will say what is going to happen. The Prosecutor is going to summarise your statement. Thereafter, she will ask you whether this is, indeed, what you stated. It might be that some documents will be submitted to you for you to comment on them. As a rule, in this type of proceedings, the accused then asks questions of the witness. It so happens that Mr. Seselj, the accused in this case, has decided, for various principles -- reasons, including reasons of principle, not to cross-examine 92 ter witnesses. In spite of this situation, the Judges you have in front of you, whose mission is to make a determination, after examination of the evidence, as to the guilt or innocence of the accused, the Judges have to look at your statement, ask questions of you, if need be, in order to shed light on specific points contained in your statement. We will, therefore, possibly ask you questions, questions that could have been asked by the accused. But since he does not do that, the Judges may ask questions that could have been put either by the accused or by the Prosecution. Do your best to answer the questions. The questions deal with events that go back 15 years, and it would be understandable that you would not be able to be very accurate as to dates, names, and locations. That is understandable. Once this stage of the proceeding is completed, the Prosecutor, as part of what is called redirect, if she feels that some questions put by the accused, if any, or when the accused puts questions, or by the Judges, raises issues that have to be specified, the Prosecutor can put questions that refer to the questions put beforehand. So this is how this testimony is going to take place. We have breaks every hour and a half, but rest assured this is not going to go on for days on end. We should be finished by the end of the day. However, if at any time you do not feel well - that can happen - do not hesitate to say so and we'll have a short break for you to have a rest. So this was what I had to tell you for this to take place as best as possible for you, because you come from far away. It may not be the first time you are a witness, but testifying in a court of law is always something really quite stressful for witnesses, and we do our best to make sure that things unfold as smoothly as possible. I now give the floor to the Prosecutor for the beginning of her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will start by reading a short summary of the witness's evidence. The witness is an inhabitant of Vocin, married to a Croatian. From 1973 until August 1991, she worked as a cleaning lady. In 1990, about two-thirds of the population of Vocin were Serb and the rest were Croats. The witness noted that after the elections in 1990, ethnic tension arose. The different ethnic groups began to accuse each other of being Ustashas or Chetniks. On 14 January 1991, the head of the SDS party visited Vocin. A woman who was present at his speech told the witness that he asked the Serbs to stick together and that the surrounding area, including Vocin, would be part of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. In the morning of 19 August 1991, the witness, on her way to work, was stopped by a masked, armed man who ordered her to return home. She could hear automatic weapons fire in the area of Prevenda Street, where most of the Croats lived. Later, all Croats were ordered to gather by a cross on Prevenda Street and were told to surrender their weapons, else they would be killed. From 19 August 1991, Vocin was blockaded and the witness was not allowed to work. Approximately eight or ten days following the blockade, armed local Serbs in JNA uniforms came to the witness' house and looted it. From this day onwards, there was a big Serb flag hoisted at the Vocin police station. The Croat flag was already taken away several days earlier. Following the escape of many young people from Vocin, the Serbs ordered that a list be made of Croats living in the village. The Croats were warned that if one of them ran away, all would be killed. On 22nd October 1991, many Croatian men were detained in the basement of the Vocin bank. That morning, armed local Serbs in civilian clothes took away the witness' husband. Later, the witness went to the police station and found out that her husband had been taken to the bank. A police officer told her that she should bring food and clothes for him, as he would spend the night there. The police officer also said that, "Since Serbs were arrested and were held in Slatina, that is why your people must be held here." However, the witness' husband was released that evening. He informed the witness what had happened in the basement. A man had an epileptic seizure. A doctor was called and ordered that everyone should be released due to the bad conditions in the basement. Two Croat inhabitants disappeared on 22nd October 1991. Vocin was relatively calm until November 1991, when more soldiers arrived from Serbia. The witness saw them arrive in civilian buses. They were based in the elementary school and the bowling hall. The local inhabitants tried to avoid contact with these soldiers, but they contacted the local inhabitants once in a while, asking for alcohol. The witness states that they were dressed in all kinds of clothes, including a mismatch of old JNA uniforms and civilian clothing. The witness recalls seeing them wearing all types of hats, including JNA caps with the five-pointed star, black knitted caps, and fur hats. Some wore badges with eagles, some with skulls and crossbones. They all carried weapons with bayonets and carried one or more knives. They presented themselves as Seselj's men and Arkan's men. Some of them told the witness that they came from all over Serbia, including Belgrade, Nis, Novi Sad. They said that they came to Vocin to kill Ustashas. One of them said that he came from the prison in Nis and that if he served one month on the frontline, his sentence would be reduced by one year. On 3rd or 4th December 1991, four young Croat men, who had to perform labour for the Serbs in Vocin, were ordered to do some work in Ceralije. Approximately four days after the young men went missing, three other people who lived close to the witness' home were killed. The witness and her husband left Vocin on 11 December 1991. Many buildings in the village, including the bus station, fire brigade, police station, and bowling hall, were on fire. The witness saw a number of dead bodies in the village, and all the killed people were civilians and most of them were older people. Later, the witness also heard that the Catholic Church of Vocin was destroyed by an explosion. In September 1992, the witness moved back to Vocin to discover that her house was totally destroyed. Your Honours, this concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please ask the witness whether she, indeed, signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Madam Witness, did you give a statement in 2001 to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: And then, in 2002, when you met with the representatives of this Tribunal, did you make corrections to your first statement?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I didn't have anything to correct. Everything was truthful. I did talk to the representatives, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: And you had given a supplementary statement in 2002?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review your written statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Usher, could you please hand out the hard copy of the English version of the statement dated 12 December 2001, thank you, bearing ERN number 0200-8618 - 0200-8625.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Madam Witness, could you look at the first page of the English version. Can you identify your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can you flip through the pages and look at page 6 of this statement. Can you identify your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Now, Usher, can you please hand out the hard copy of the B/C/S version of the supplementary statement. It's dated 6 September 2002. Thank you. In the B/C/S version, the ERN is 0326-0814, which in the English version is 0307-6081.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can you identify your signature at the bottom of this statement?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Now, Usher, please, could you hand out the hard copy of the B/C/S statement, again dated 12th February 2001, thank you, bearing ERN number 0305-5362 - 0305-5369. Your Honours, the English version bears ERN number 0200-8618 - 0200-8625.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I would like to direct your attention on page 3, paragraph 1, which in the English version is located on page 3, paragraph 2. Madam Witness, page 3, paragraph 1, I will read out the relevant line for you: "On the 14th of January, 1991, a Serb called Rasko Draskovic visited the village of Vocin." Is the name accurate?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to direct your attention to page 4, second-last paragraph, which in the English version is page 5, paragraph 1. I will read out the relevant line: "Everything was more or less calm until the Serbs brought other soldiers from Serbia." Who were these additional soldiers? Please describe them.

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: These were other soldiers who came from Serbia. They said, "We're Seselj's men." Some said, "We're Arkan's men." Those were the ones, the other soldiers. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Again, Madam Witness, on the same page, that is, page 4, last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: This, in the English version, Your Honours, is located on page 5, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: I will read out the relevant line: "We were trying very hard avoiding meeting them and have any contact with them." Why did you avoid meeting them?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Well, because they were, how shall I put it, unpleasant. They were saying, "We're here to kill the Ustashas. We're Chetniks. You have to obey us. We'll tell you what to do, and you've got to tow the line." They were very unpleasant, they wanted stuff to drink all the time, and we had to get it for them. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, on page 6 of your statement, second-last paragraph, which in the English version is on page 6, paragraph 5, I will read out the relevant line: "We stayed in Banja Luka for seven days." Madam Witness, is this accurate, the number of days?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't stay for seven days. I don't know how I ended up saying this. We just spent the night in Banja Luka, and the next day we took the bus to Zagreb. But there was another group who did stay for seven days. My husband's sister-in-law, she stayed for seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Madam Witness, with the clarifications you've just specified, does that statement accurately reflect your recollection of the events described in it?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: And if you were asked questions about those events today, would you give the same answers that are contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answers are what they are. I don't know how or why I said the thing about the seven days. I think I was probably asked how long people, generally speaking, stayed in Banja Luka, and I said, "Seven days." I don't think she asked about me or my husband specifically, because we travelled back the next day. We spent this one night at the bus terminal, and then we returned to Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, at this point, we would move for the admission of 65 ter number 5011, which contains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P608, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a number of questions to put to you, based on your written statement and based on paragraphs 73, 75, and 77 of the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, and based also on the indictment. I'm saying this for everybody to be able to follow my questions. One point of clarification, Witness. We believe that you were a Serb, married to a Croat; but on the 6th of September, 2002, you stated that you were Bulgarian. So are you a Serb or are you a Bulgarian?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Bulgarian by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you were born in a Bulgarian settlement?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes, straddling the Bulgarian border. But this was Bulgarian territory until just before the previous war, and then a border was created running down the middle of our village, so half the village was now Serb and half the village was Bulgarian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And later on, did you have a Bulgarian passport?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: No, I never had one. I got married, I came to Vocin, and I had Bulgarian ID. But after my wedding and after I changed my name, I moved to Croatia. At this point, I got Croatian ID. The Bulgarian one was held back by the municipal authorities where the new one was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you stated that on the 19th of August, 1991, soldiers arrived in the town of Vocin. Can you tell us again, who were these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: I can't distinguish between the groups. I know that they would walk down our street, introducing themselves as Seselj's men or Arkan's men, but I have no idea who brought them there or, indeed, who welcomed them. This is something we didn't know at the time, nor, indeed, did we ever dare to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you heard one of these soldiers say, "I am a Seselj man," or, "I am an Arkan man"?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I would talk to them out in the street. I would tell them that I was from Serbia and that they shouldn't touch any of us. Then they said, "I'm from Serbia, too. I'm one of Seselj's men." Another one came up and said, "I'm one of Arkan's men." So they did point this out on a number of occasions, but it's not like I could afford to spend a long time talking to them. We tried to get out of their way. We did our best not to be in touch with them too much. We were scared, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You saw them, because they remained there for a while. Was their behaviour the type of behaviour you expect from a soldier or was it the sort of behaviour you would not expect from a soldier?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: No. They weren't really acting like soldiers. They were acting like they were a law unto themselves. As I said, I even wasn't that scared. My husband was far more scared than I was. I thought it best to try and protect him, and whenever we needed to talk to these soldiers, I was the one to go because my husband was too scared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You said that they arrived in August, so you saw them in August. Did you also see them in September, in October, in November, and December, until the date of your departure? Were these men there throughout this time?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: It wasn't in August that they arrived. Our village was occupied in August by the local Serbs. This occurred on the 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did Seselj's men and Arkan's men arrive, exactly?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think they arrived sometime in September, possibly early in October, but I can't be specific about the date. I don't remember. One thing is certain, it wasn't in August. It was sometime in September, possibly early October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his filings, the Prosecutor has stated that in November or December 1991, a group of volunteers of the Serb Radical Party killed four Croats after having forced them to bring ammunition to the frontline or to the battlefield, and that's to be found at footnote 223. I'm saying that for those who could be interested. So how did you know that four Croat men were killed by volunteers of the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Those were my neighbours. The sin of my "kuma." They went out into the field to pick some corn, it was Jovica Todorovic's field; and then on their way back, someone stopped them. We don't know who it was. They were on a tractor, and they said they should give them a hand to travel back from Vocin to Ceralije, to unload some ammunition or something. So they got onto the truck and they left together. They never came back. We had no idea what became of them. It went on like that for three or four days, and then we learned that they'd been killed near Gaj, which is by the river. Now, who was it that took them away on this tractor? We never learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What you've said raises a lot of questions. These four young men were arrested and climbed onto a tractor. Who arrested them, exactly, who arrested them? Were they arrested by Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know .

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: We still don't know. My "kuma" doesn't know either. The neighbours, too, would like to know who it was who took them away and killed, but this is something that cannot be known. Only the person who did it knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the Prosecutor wrote the following, I'm going to read it out very slowly: "At the end of November or at the beginning of December 1991, a group of volunteers of the SRS/SCP killed four young Croat men after having forced them to bring ammunition to the battlefield." Footnote 223, Witness 1119 and Witness 018. These young men then brought ammunition to the battlefield. Earlier on, you told us they were found dead near Gaj, near the river. Could they have been killed during fighting or because the ammunition they carried exploded, or is it also possible that they were killed by those men who were escorting them? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: I know that they were killed by those who took them away from Vocin, because they never even got near the frontline. The entire area in which they were killed was Serb occupied. They never reached the frontline. They were killed a short distance from Gaj, near the river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also can see that you're mentioned in Prosecution filings, because apparently in December, when you returned to Vocin, you took part in the funerals of 45 people killed in Hum and Vocin. Do you remember funerals for 45 people who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: They picked up their dead bodies and took them first to Slatina. There was a mine-clearing operation in Vocin, and after that all the bodies were returned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now turn to some parts of your statement. There's one thing I'd like to know. In Vocin, all these soldiers or volunteers, did they have a commander? Did they have someone commanding them; and if so, who was it, provided you know, of course?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably had some commanders, but I don't know their names and I don't know who they were over in Vocin, but I'm sure they have commanders. No doubt about that. They didn't just come out of nowhere, you know. Somebody must have sent them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see JNA officers in the streets dressed in military uniforms, with their five-pointed star, with ranks, insignia? Did you see any officers, provided you can distinguish a soldier for an officer? If you can't or if you don't know the difference, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: I think I can distinguish, but at the time in Vocin, the soldiers and the officers had withdrawn to Zvecevo Hotel. I'm not sure what the distance is. I think about ten kilometres between Vocin and Zvecevo. So they were over there because that's where they had withdrawn to. There were no officers in Vocin. They would sometimes go to the Staff there. Once, my husband and I went to the National Staff in Vocin, complaining that we were no longer able to sleep in our own home and requesting some form of protection or to be given a pass so that we could rejoin our children. It was then that I saw a soldier who had just returned from Zvecevo. I don't know what he was there for. I just know that I saw him. I know that occasionally soldiers did go to the Staff at Vocin, but they weren't permanently stationed in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could all the other microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. We are receiving an enormous amount of background noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are a few political references in your statement. You say, for instance, that in January, on the 14th of January, 1991, a Serb, Rasko Draskovic, came to Vocin, and you said of him that he was the leader of the Serbian political party. This is what I would like to know about the municipality of Vocin: What was its political affiliation in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Vocin, in 1991, it was rather Serb. They held it, and they led the way with all the proposals and orders. They were in charge all the way. As to this man who came, Jovan Draskovic, he arrived before the occupation. He arrived on the 14th of January, and they placed some wreaths to honour the victims of the previous war and their victims who can be killed in Vocin and Komatnik [phoen]. He held a speech on something, I'm not really sure. All sorts of things wer being said, but I wasn't there myself to hear exactly what it was that he said in his address on the 14th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prior to the 19th of August or on that date, was the Croatian flag raised at some time during the day?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: The Croatian flag flew in Vocin all the time until the 19th of August, when our local Serbs occupied the village. It was then that they took the Croatian flag down and hoisted their own, at least that was the case with the police station, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In August 1991, to your knowledge, which was the state that had jurisdiction over Vocin? Was it Yugoslavia or was it Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Yugoslavia, until the election. Yugoslavia, until the election. After the election, there was a turnaround and the separation begun. There was no more Yugoslavia and people were saying all sorts of things, until the occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I saw that your husband had a 7.65 pistol. Why did he have such a weapon?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Because the police was my employer, and I asked to be assigned a pistol. I would leave home --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the witness. Could all the other microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. We are receiving an enormous amount of background noise, on account of which we're not able to hear the witness properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the main reason for you to leave the municipality of Vocin?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you mind repeating, please, because the interpreters could not hear you. I asked you why you left Vocin. Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: We had to leave Vocin, because if we had stayed, they would have killed us, along with everyone else that they killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said in your statement that you left Vocin on the 11th of December, 1991, so this is the date you indicated. We know that you went somewhere else and then you returned to Vocin. I'm asking you now why you turned back and returned to Vocin.

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: We spent two days in Macute with Nikola Pavlovic, and then they were told to run and try to escape because the Ustashas were on their way there. My husband and I duly returned to Vocin to release our livestock. We had a cow that was locked up in a shed, and we wanted to make sure the cow was released and so the shed wouldn't be burned down. My husband pulled a blanket over his head because he --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The interpreters cannot hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the house like when you returned?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: It was ruined. The church had been mined and demolished. There were the tiles falling off the roof, and there was a fire burning inside the house. More than half the house had burnt down, and it was no longer inhabitable. Instead, we stayed in the flat in Slatina until September 1992. Then there was this state-run reconstruction programme, as a result of which the state rebuilt our home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me move now to my last question. You say that you left Vocin on the 11th of December, 1991. It would appear that in November, sometime before, Mr. Seselj went to Vocin. Did you hear about it or were you not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: We'd heard about his arrival in Vocin, but we didn't see him ourselves and we didn't really know. We heard people talk about that, talk about him having visited Vocin, but we don't know when he was there or, indeed, what he told anyone there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you can't say anything about his visit.

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: I can't. If I knew, I'd tell you, I'd tell you what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Witness. My fellow Judges don't have questions. I'll therefore ask the Prosecutor whether they have additional questions only connected to the questions I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we have to correct the transcript. On page 43, line 8, it is mentioned the name "Jovan Draskovic," as it's written here. I heard the witness saying "Jovan Raskovic." I think it's wrong in the transcript and it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, would you mind repeating the name of this person called "Draskovic"? What was his first name, what was his surname?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Jovan Draskovic, no. The first time around I didn't really know the name, but then I found out later that it was Jovan Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It gets complicated. Is it "Raskovic" or "Draskovic"?

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: Raskovic, Jovan. But I'm not very good with names. I may occasionally drop a letter or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, you see, in your written statement, we see "Rasko Draskovic."

utterances.speaker: JULKA MARETIC
utterances.text: I didn't really know at the time. I couldn't tell them for sure. I know that he was the man named Drasko, Rasko, whatever; but then later they told me that his first name was Jovan Raskovic. Draskovic, Raskovic, easy to mix up, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you satisfied with the answer, Mr. Mussemeyer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Not 100 per cent, but it may remain like this because we had other witnesses who testified about the same event and they recalled the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Madam Prosecutor, did you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, on behalf of the Trial Chamber and in my own name, I thank you for coming from so far to testify here. I can only wish you a safe trip back home. I'll ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one objection to voice after the witness leaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may leave the courtroom, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know my position in principle concerning testimony under 92 ter, so I will not repeat it; however, what the Prosecutor staged today is a scandal. If we had the same application of Rule 92 ter in this procedure, then it would be inadmissible to admit the documents tendered by the Prosecutor. We have the first statement of this witness of the 12th of February, 2001, in Slatina. Then we have a certification, an acknowledgment, that under what was then Rule 92 bis, an authorised officer of the Registry went to Vocin and asked the witness, at the police station, to confirm her signature and the contents. Then it says here that, by making the declaration, the witness confirmed the veracity of the written statement she had made, and this was signed by an investigator of the OTP, an interpreter of the ICTY, the presiding officer Frederick Swinnen, and the witness, under Rule 92 bis. Now we have the third document of the same date, 6 September, 2002, which introduces significant modifications. You have noticed that the witness is not Serbian; she's Bulgarian. She confirmed that certain things were committed by local Serbs. She was more emphatic about that than earlier; and, allegedly, she added at the end, which she repeated here, that some of those newly-come soldiers from Serbia said that they were Seselj's men, while others said that they were Arkan's men. We established for a fact today that Arkan's men were never present there during the war. We have had a number of witnesses from Western Slavonia, and I believe that by now it has become an undisputed fact. Seselj's men, that is, volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, were present, and they were there in large numbers, and there were some others as well. That's not in question. Now, the first question that arises is: On whose suggestion did the witness correct this after 18 months? This interview was conducted in a police station, so we can understand that this was suggested. I don't mind that she was led to correct this, but the form of this document is such that it should not be admissible. It doesn't state who took the statement, under what circumstances, or anything. It just says this is an additional statement. Any additional statement must follow the same format as the main witness statement. This form has not been observed here, and we can only take the Prosecutor's word for it. Of course, the witness confirmed her signature on the paper, but you can see her intellectual and social profile and you can see that she's amenable to all sorts of manipulation. I do not doubt that she was honest and sincere when she spoke here, completely unaware of all the mischief by the Prosecution. Although this Prosecution document does not damage me in any way, I do object to its admission. My second objection is this: You remember, Mr. President, that one indictment was brought against me in 2003, then it was extended in 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Dr. Seselj. It might be better for Mr. Mundis to react to the first objection, because now you're moving on to something else. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to influence you in your answers, but let me observe that the document of the 6th of September, 2002, arrived in mysterious ways; and it's also noted that among the signatures, you did not have the name of the OTP staff member who was present or was absent, or whether it was the Registrar. It's a bit unclear. You must have noticed that yourself. This being said, what did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The point that caused me to rise to my feet seems to be a recurring one, and that is that we need to put clearly on the record the Prosecution position that much of what Mr. Seselj has just said could have been the subject of cross-examination. He has knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently made a decision on his behalf not to cross-examine these witnesses; and, consequently, he has waived the right to do so. Having taken that step, it is inappropriate for him to then comment on matters that could have and should have been put to the witness when they were in the courtroom. This new practice of running commentary or making statements about what the witness did, or could have done, or could have said, or might have said had she asked questions about that is, in our respectful view, an inappropriate way to proceed, and I want to make that very clear on the record. Mr. Seselj has repeatedly indicated as a matter of principle he will not cross-examine these witnesses. So be it. It is not then appropriate for him to be making comments, or to be speculating, or to be challenging statements which he didn't object to when they were tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, but the legal problem is as follows: The 92 ter proceeding is that after the summary, the OTP seeks to tender the document, an exhibit number is given and the document is tendered into evidence, and then we have cross-examination. Mr. Seselj decided not to cross-examine. Very well. Then there are questions by the Judges, and during this stage, it could be that new elements may appear. I saw and I was wondering whether she was Bulgarian or Serb, following which the testimony is completed. But in the view of the Trial Chamber, the accused is free to object to the final admission of the document if the accused, through what the witness may have said in their answers, whether he saw that there could be some problems. He then could object, saying, "I'm against the admission of the document on various grounds," which he specifies. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's certainly no problem with him objecting to the admissibility of the documents. There is a problem when he starts speculating about the witness' testimony, when he didn't put questions to the witness. That is fundamentally unfair for him to wait until the witness leaves the courtroom and then to speculate about what would have been proper subjects for him to cross-examine her on, and that's simply why I rose to my feet.
